News global nation business lifestyle entertainment technology sports opinion LATEST NEWS STORIES HEADLINES METRO REGIONS NATION WORLD CDN NEWSLETTER www / West Philippine Sea West Philippine Sea West PH Sea: Oban urges 5-year plan to uphold South China Sea rules By: Kenneth Christiane Basilio - Reporter / @kl_basilioINQ INQUIRER.net / 10:30 AM November 16, 2026 Share: MANILA, Philippines – National Security Adviser Eduardo Oban Jr. said late Sunday that 2031 should serve as a target horizon for strategic planning to ensure the South China Sea remains governed by international rules rather than military might, amid China’s coercive actions in the disputed waters.
“If we want to influence the South China Sea in 2031, we must recognize that strategic competition has changed,” Oban said in his opening remarks at the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea.
His remarks came as China continued to exert maritime pressure in the South China Sea, a strategic waterway through which trillions of dollars in trade pass annually and where Philippine and Chinese vessels have been involved in recurring collisions and confrontations.
Beijing’s claim is based on a nine-dash line map dating to the 1940s that encompasses the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone (EEZ), part of which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. A United Nations-backed tribunal invalidated China’s claim in 2016, ruling that it had no legal basis under international law.
Oban described the South China Sea as no longer just a contested waterway, but rather an “arena where military power, economic security, technology, information, international law and diplomatic influence intersect.”
“Strategic competition must never make coercion an accepted means of managing differences,” he said. “Preventing armed conflict remains essential, but preventing the gradual erosion of regional maritime order is primordial.”
And he noted that a five-year horizon through 2031 will prove decisive in determining whether international rules prevail over “coercion and unilateral actions” in the South China Sea.
“Several developments will shape this period, including China’s continuing military modernization, the Philippines’ next national security planning cycle, and Asean’s implementation of regional economic and security priorities,” Oban said.

For the Philippines, he said, the path to 2031 requires forging deeper security alliances without sacrificing diplomatic boundaries, while bolstering regional mechanisms for maritime safety, including that Asean and its partners must translate commitments into practical arrangements to prevent incidents at sea.
Building greater national resilience by fortifying the country’s physical and digital infrastructure to reduce systemic vulnerabilities should also be a priority, he added.
